question.worked_solution:
We start by sketching the two intervals $(-1,2)$ and $[0,3)$ separately:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/a5a6b966c5d98863cfed20ccb13f3a1ca5413887f228f091d504bb7cd0001b37.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/823bf1d62aadc91ac15e52260a9919622358144865f0522f34389d48f8c11273.png)

The intersection $(-1,2)\cap [0,3)$ represents the values that are in both intervals. So, it can be graphed by finding where the two intervals overlap:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191341/assets/9c7ea77f9699601b97ff38a886af6418b44fa9568009aaa4b36be17efa03cbee.png)

Thus, $(-1,2)\cap [0,3)=[0,2).$ This corresponds to the inequality $0\le x<2.$
